questions.q: What is the SI unit of the amount of a substance?
questions.explanation: The mole is the SI base unit for amount of substance; it counts elementary entities such as atoms or molecules.

questions.q: How many atoms are present in exactly 12 g of carbon-12?
questions.explanation: 12 g of carbon-12 is one mole, which contains Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10^23, of atoms.

questions.q: How many moles of water are present in 36 g of water? (Molar mass of H2O = 18 g/mol)
questions.explanation: Moles = 36 g / 18 g per mol = 2 mol.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO3? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CaCO3 is 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 g/mol, so 0.25 mol has a mass of 25 g.

questions.q: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Mole ratio C : H : O = 40/12 : 6.7/1 : 53.3/16 = 3.33 : 6.7 : 3.33 = 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH2O.

questions.q: 2 mol of hydrogen gas and 2 mol of oxygen gas are made to react completely according to 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. What mass of water is formed? (H2O = 18 g/mol)
questions.explanation: 2 mol H2 needs only 1 mol O2, so H2 is the limiting reagent and gives 2 mol of water = 36 g.

questions.q: What is the molality of a solution made by dissolving 18 g of glucose (molar mass 180 g/mol) in 500 g of water?
questions.explanation: Moles of glucose = 18/180 = 0.1 mol; mass of solvent = 0.5 kg; molality = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 mol per kg.

questions.q: Calculate the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 4 g of NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol) in water to make 500 mL of solution.
questions.explanation: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, so 0.1 mol in 0.5 L gives 0.2 M.

questions.q: How many significant figures are there in the measurement 0.00450 g? Give a reason.
questions.answer: Three significant figures (4, 5 and the final 0).
keyPoints: Trailing zero after a non-zero digit in a decimal number is significant
questions.explanation: Zeros that only locate the decimal point at the start are not counted, but the final zero shows measured precision.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered the atomic nucleus through the gold foil scattering experiment?
questions.explanation: Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment showed that most of the atom's mass and positive charge is in a tiny nucleus.

questions.q: An atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 23 - 11 = 12.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that the third shell (n = 3) can hold?
questions.explanation: The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n^2 = 2 × 9 = 18.

questions.q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, ml) is NOT permissible for an electron in an atom?
questions.explanation: For a given n, l can have values 0 to n-1 only, so l = 2 is not possible when n = 2.

questions.q: What is the ground state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
questions.explanation: Chromium prefers a half-filled 3d subshell, so one 4s electron shifts to 3d, giving [Ar] 3d5 4s1.

questions.q: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 5 × 10^14 Hz? (h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J s)
In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the radius of the third orbit is how many times the radius of the first orbit?
questions.explanation: Orbit radius is proportional to n^2, so r3/r1 = 3^2/1^2 = 9.

questions.q: State Pauli's exclusion principle and explain what it implies for the maximum number of electrons in one orbital.
questions.answer: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers, so an orbital can hold at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins.
keyPoints: No two electrons share identical n, l, ml and ms
Electrons in one orbital differ in spin quantum number
Maximum occupancy of an orbital is 2
questions.explanation: Two electrons in one orbital already share n, l and ml, so they must differ in ms (+1/2 and -1/2).

questions.q: Find the number of radial nodes and angular nodes in a 3p orbital.
questions.explanation: For 3p, n = 3 and l = 1, so use n - l - 1 for radial nodes and l for angular nodes.

questions.q: According to the modern periodic law, the properties of elements are a periodic function of their
questions.explanation: Moseley's work led to the modern periodic law, which is based on atomic number.

questions.q: Which of the following has the largest atomic radius?
questions.explanation: Atomic radius increases down a group as more shells are added, and caesium is lowest among these in group 1.

questions.q: Among Na, Mg, Ne and O, which has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Neon has a stable, filled octet and a high effective nuclear charge, so removing an electron is hardest.

questions.q: Among the halogens F, Cl, Br and I, which has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is so small that electron-electron repulsion reduces its value, so chlorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy.

questions.q: Which of the isoelectronic species O2-, F-, Na+ and Mg2+ has the largest ionic radius?
questions.explanation: All have 10 electrons, but O2- has the fewest protons (8), so the weakest pull on the electrons and the largest radius.

questions.q: An element has the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5. In which period and group does it lie?
questions.explanation: The outermost shell is n = 3, so period 3; it has 7 valence electrons, so it is in group 17 (a halogen).

questions.q: The first ionisation enthalpy of boron is lower than that of beryllium mainly because
options: boron has a larger atomic radius than beryllium
the electron lost by boron comes from a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and shielded by the 2s electrons
boron has a smaller nuclear charge than beryllium
questions.explanation: The 2p electron of boron is less penetrating and easier to remove than the 2s electron of beryllium, even though boron has the larger nuclear charge.

questions.q: Why is a cation always smaller than its parent atom?
questions.answer: Loss of electrons reduces electron-electron repulsion and often removes a whole shell, while the nuclear charge stays the same, so the remaining electrons are pulled in more strongly.
keyPoints: Fewer electrons, same number of protons
Higher effective nuclear charge per electron
Often the outermost shell is lost
questions.explanation: With the same nuclear charge holding fewer electrons, the electron cloud contracts.

questions.q: Why is the second ionisation enthalpy of sodium much larger than its first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.answer: After the first electron is removed Na+ has the stable neon configuration; the next electron must be taken from an inner, closer shell held by a higher effective nuclear charge.
keyPoints: Electron comes from an inner shell nearer the nucleus
Much greater energy needed than for the single 3s electron
questions.explanation: The first electron is a lone, well-shielded 3s electron, whereas the second is a tightly held 2p electron.

questions.q: What is the shape of a methane (CH4) molecule?
questions.explanation: Carbon in methane is sp3 hybridised with four bond pairs, giving a tetrahedral shape with 109.5 degree angles.

questions.q: Which type of bond is present in sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, and the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions are held by electrostatic attraction.

questions.q: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene, C2H4?
questions.explanation: Each carbon forms three sigma bonds and one pi bond, which means sp2 hybridisation.

questions.q: According to molecular orbital theory, what is the bond order of the O2 molecule?
questions.explanation: O2 has 10 bonding and 6 antibonding electrons, so bond order = (10 - 6)/2 = 2.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules has a zero dipole moment?
questions.explanation: CO2 is linear, so the two equal C=O bond dipoles cancel each other.

questions.q: What is the shape of the XeF4 molecule?
questions.explanation: Xenon has four bond pairs and two lone pairs; the lone pairs sit opposite each other, giving a square planar molecule.

questions.q: The bond angles in CH4, NH3 and H2O decrease in the order 109.5 degrees, 107 degrees and 104.5 degrees. This is best explained by the fact that
options: lone pairs repel bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel one another
carbon is sp3 hybridised while oxygen is sp hybridised
questions.explanation: The number of lone pairs increases from 0 to 1 to 2, and lone pair-bond pair repulsion squeezes the H-X-H angle.

questions.q: Define bond order and give its value for the nitrogen molecule N2.
questions.answer: Bond order is half the difference between the number of electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals; for N2 it is 3.
keyPoints: N2 has 10 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons
Bond order of N2 = 3, a triple bond
questions.explanation: A higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond, which explains the very high stability of N2.

questions.q: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulphide although H2S has the larger molar mass?
questions.answer: Oxygen is highly electronegative and small, so water molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which need much more energy to break; H2S does not hydrogen-bond appreciably.
keyPoints: H2S has only weak dipole and van der Waals forces
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding outweighs the effect of larger mass on van der Waals forces.

questions.q: At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is inversely proportional to its
questions.explanation: This is Boyle's law: P × V is constant at constant temperature.

questions.q: What is the value of absolute zero on the Celsius scale?
questions.explanation: Absolute zero, 0 K, corresponds to -273.15 °C.

questions.q: What is the pressure of 2 mol of an ideal gas in a 10 L vessel at 300 K? (R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1)
A gas mixture has 2 mol of N2 and 3 mol of O2 at a total pressure of 5 atm. What is the partial pressure of N2?
questions.explanation: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = (2/5) × 5 = 2 atm.

questions.q: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 300 K and constant pressure. What volume will it occupy at 450 K?
questions.explanation: By Charles's law V2 = V1 × T2/T1 = 2.0 × 450/300 = 3.0 L.

questions.q: Which gas effuses fastest under the same conditions?
questions.explanation: By Graham's law rate is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass, and H2 has the lowest molar mass.

questions.q: A gas X diffuses at half the rate of methane (molar mass 16 g/mol) under the same conditions. What is the molar mass of X?
questions.explanation: rate(X)/rate(CH4) = sqrt(16/M) = 1/2, so 16/M = 1/4 and M = 64 g/mol.

questions.q: Real gases deviate strongly from ideal behaviour at very high pressure mainly because
options: the temperature of the gas always falls
the volume occupied by the molecules becomes comparable to the volume of the container
the molecules lose mass when compressed
questions.explanation: The ideal gas model assumes negligible molecular volume, which fails when the gas is compressed so much that molecular volume is a significant fraction of the total.

questions.q: How many moles of gas are present in 5.6 L of a gas at 273 K and 1 atm? (Molar volume at these conditions = 22.4 L/mol)
keyPoints: One mole occupies 22.4 L at 273 K and 1 atm
questions.explanation: Divide the given volume by the molar volume: 5.6/22.4 = 0.25.

questions.q: Which of the following is an intensive property?
questions.explanation: Density does not depend on the amount of matter, whereas volume, mass and enthalpy do.

questions.q: A system that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings is called a(n)
questions.explanation: An isolated system cannot exchange matter or energy; a closed system can exchange energy only.

questions.q: A system absorbs 100 J of heat and does 40 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in internal energy (using the IUPAC sign convention)?
questions.explanation: ΔU = q + w = +100 J + (-40 J) = +60 J, since work done by the system is negative.

questions.q: For the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), the relation between ΔH and ΔU is
questions.explanation: ΔH = ΔU + Δng RT and Δng = 2 - 4 = -2, so ΔH = ΔU - 2RT.

questions.q: Given C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = -394 kJ/mol and CO(g) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = -283 kJ/mol, what is the enthalpy change for C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g)?
questions.explanation: By Hess's law, ΔH = -394 - (-283) = -111 kJ/mol.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +30 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/(K mol). Above what temperature does it become spontaneous?
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS < 0 when T > 30000 J / 100 J K^-1 = 300 K.

questions.q: For which of the following processes is the entropy change of the system negative?
questions.explanation: Condensation makes the system more ordered, so entropy decreases, whereas the other three increase disorder.

questions.q: The combustion of 1 mol of methane releases 890 kJ. How much heat is released by burning 8 g of methane? (CH4 = 16 g/mol)
questions.explanation: 8 g is 0.5 mol, so heat released = 0.5 × 890 = 445 kJ.

questions.q: Explain why the enthalpy of neutralisation of any strong acid with a strong base is nearly constant at about -57 kJ per mole of water formed.
questions.answer: Strong acids and bases are completely ionised, so the only net reaction is H+ + OH- → H2O, which is the same for every pair.
keyPoints: Strong acids and bases dissociate completely
Spectator ions do not take part
Net change is H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l)
questions.explanation: Since the net reaction is identical, the heat released per mole of water is nearly the same.

questions.q: According to Le Chatelier's principle, if the concentration of a reactant is increased at equilibrium, the equilibrium
options: shifts in the forward direction to use up the added reactant
questions.explanation: The system opposes the change by consuming some of the added reactant, forming more product.

questions.q: What is the expression for Kc for the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)?
questions.explanation: Kc is products raised to their coefficients divided by reactants raised to their coefficients.

questions.q: What is the pH of a 0.001 M solution of HCl at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: HCl is a strong acid, so [H+] = 10^-3 M and pH = 3.

questions.q: For which of the following reactions is Kp equal to Kc?
questions.explanation: Kp = Kc (RT)^Δng, and Δng = 0 only for H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI.

questions.q: For H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) the equilibrium constant is 50 at a given temperature. What is the constant for 2HI(g) ⇌ H2(g) + I2(g) at that temperature?
questions.explanation: Reversing the reaction inverts K, so K = 1/50 = 0.02.

questions.q: What is the pH of a 0.01 M NaOH solution at 25 °C?
In which of the following is the solubility of AgCl lowest?
questions.explanation: The common ion Cl- in NaCl suppresses dissolution of AgCl, while NH3 even increases it by forming a complex.

questions.q: Which of the following mixtures acts as an acidic buffer?
questions.explanation: A weak acid with its salt of a strong base resists pH change; HCl and HNO3 are strong acids, so they do not buffer.

questions.q: For N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [N2O4] = 0.2 M and [NO2] = 0.4 M. Calculate Kc.
questions.explanation: Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the expression with NO2 squared.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H2SO4?
In terms of electron transfer, oxidation is
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons, which raises the oxidation number.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7?
In the reaction Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu, the oxidising agent is
questions.explanation: Cu2+ gains electrons and is reduced, so it is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disproportionation reaction?
questions.explanation: In H2O2 oxygen (-1) is both oxidised to O2 (0) and reduced to H2O (-2).

questions.q: In MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ → Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O, how many electrons does each MnO4- ion gain?
questions.explanation: Mn changes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons.

questions.q: What is the average oxidation number of sulphur in the tetrathionate ion in Na2S4O6?
questions.explanation: 2(+1) + 4x + 6(-2) = 0 gives 4x = 10, so x = +2.5 on average.

questions.q: Why does fluorine show only the -1 oxidation state and never a positive one in compounds?
questions.answer: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and has no d orbitals, so it always attracts the shared electrons and cannot lose electrons or expand its octet.
keyPoints: No vacant d orbitals to expand octet
questions.explanation: With every bond to a less electronegative element, fluorine takes the electrons and so is always -1.

questions.q: Explain why hydrogen peroxide can act as both an oxidising agent and a reducing agent.
questions.answer: Oxygen in H2O2 has oxidation number -1, which lies between 0 (in O2) and -2 (in H2O), so it can be raised or lowered.
keyPoints: Oxidation number of O in H2O2 is -1
Can be reduced to water or hydroxide (-2)
questions.explanation: An element in an intermediate oxidation state can both increase and decrease it.

questions.q: Which isotope of hydrogen is radioactive?
questions.explanation: Tritium (3H) is radioactive and emits beta particles, whereas protium and deuterium are stable.

questions.q: What is the formula of heavy water?
questions.explanation: Heavy water is deuterium oxide, D2O.

questions.q: Which alkali metal imparts a golden-yellow colour to a Bunsen flame?
questions.explanation: Sodium gives an intense golden-yellow flame, lithium crimson red and potassium lilac.

questions.q: What is the formula of washing soda?
questions.explanation: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O.

questions.q: Beryllium chloride is largely covalent while barium chloride is ionic. The best explanation is that
options: Be2+ is very small with high charge density, so it strongly polarises the chloride ion
beryllium has a lower ionisation enthalpy than barium
chlorine is less electronegative towards beryllium
questions.explanation: By Fajans' rules, a small, highly charged cation such as Be2+ distorts the anion's electron cloud and gives covalent character.

questions.q: Give two reasons why hydrogen is placed separately from the alkali metals in some versions of the periodic table.
questions.answer: Hydrogen is a non-metal that exists as a diatomic gas, and it can also gain one electron to form H-, unlike alkali metals.
keyPoints: Forms H- ions by gaining an electron
Much higher ionisation enthalpy than alkali metals
questions.explanation: Hydrogen resembles both group 1 (one valence electron) and group 17 (needs one electron), so it fits neither group exactly.

questions.q: What is temporary hardness of water, what causes it, and how can it be removed?
questions.answer: Temporary hardness is due to dissolved bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium and is removed by boiling, which precipitates the carbonates.
keyPoints: Boiling decomposes them to insoluble carbonates
Can also be removed by Clark's method
questions.explanation: On heating, Ca(HCO3)2 → CaCO3 + H2O + CO2, so the calcium leaves the solution.

questions.q: Write the equation for the reaction of sodium with water and explain why sodium is stored under kerosene.
questions.answer: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2. Sodium reacts vigorously with moisture and oxygen in air, so it is kept under kerosene.
keyPoints: Kerosene keeps out air and moisture
questions.explanation: Sodium is highly reactive and would otherwise catch fire or corrode in air.

questions.q: What is the correct formula of borax?
questions.explanation: Borax is sodium tetraborate decahydrate, Na2B4O7·10H2O.

questions.q: Which of the following is an allotrope of carbon?
questions.explanation: Fullerenes such as C60 are allotropes of carbon, as are diamond and graphite; the others are compounds.

questions.q: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in diamond?
questions.explanation: Each carbon is bonded to four others in a tetrahedral network, which means sp3 hybridisation.

questions.q: Anhydrous aluminium chloride exists as the dimer Al2Cl6 in the vapour state because
options: aluminium is electron-deficient and completes its octet by using lone pairs of bridging chlorine atoms
the dimer has ionic Al-Al bonds
questions.explanation: In AlCl3 aluminium has only six electrons; two molecules join through chlorine bridges that donate lone pairs.

questions.q: Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not because in graphite
options: all four electrons of carbon are held in sigma bonds
each carbon uses three electrons in sigma bonds and the fourth is delocalised between the layers
questions.explanation: Graphite has sp2 carbon in layers, and the leftover p electrons are delocalised and free to move along the layers.

questions.q: Why is carbon monoxide poisonous to humans?
questions.answer: CO binds to the iron in haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and blocking oxygen transport.
keyPoints: Oxygen carrying capacity of blood falls
questions.explanation: The body's tissues become starved of oxygen, causing headache, unconsciousness and possibly death.

questions.q: What is the inert pair effect? Give one example from group 14.
questions.answer: It is the reluctance of the two outer s electrons to take part in bonding in heavier p-block elements, so a lower oxidation state is more stable; for example Pb2+ is more stable than Pb4+.
keyPoints: ns2 electrons stay unused in heavier elements
Lower oxidation state becomes more stable
Example: Pb(II) more stable than Pb(IV)
questions.explanation: Poor shielding by d and f electrons makes the s electrons held tightly, so they are not lost easily.

questions.q: Boric acid is a weak monobasic Lewis acid. Write the equation showing how it behaves in water.
keyPoints: Boron accepts a hydroxide ion from water (Lewis acid)
questions.explanation: It does not donate H+ itself; it accepts OH- from water, which leaves H3O+ in solution.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CH2OH?
questions.explanation: A three-carbon chain with an -OH on the first carbon is propan-1-ol.

questions.q: The functional group present in a ketone is
options: a carbonyl group joined to two carbon atoms
questions.explanation: A ketone has a C=O group bonded to two carbon atoms, unlike an aldehyde where one is hydrogen.

questions.q: Among alkyl carbocations, which is the most stable?
questions.explanation: A tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three alkyl groups through the inductive effect and hyperconjugation.

questions.q: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in propene, CH2=CH-CH3?
questions.explanation: There are 6 C-H sigma bonds, 2 C-C sigma bonds (one in C=C) = 8 sigma, and one pi bond in the double bond.

questions.q: Which of the following is the strongest acid?
questions.explanation: The electron-withdrawing chlorine (-I effect) stabilises the carboxylate ion, whereas alkyl groups destabilise it.

questions.q: Distinguish between homolytic and heterolytic bond fission.
questions.answer: In homolytic fission the shared pair is split equally, one electron to each atom, forming free radicals; in heterolytic fission one atom takes both electrons, forming a cation and an anion.
keyPoints: Homolytic: one electron to each fragment, gives free radicals
Heterolytic: both electrons go to one atom, gives ions
questions.explanation: The type of fission determines whether the reaction proceeds through radicals or ionic intermediates.

questions.q: Write the structural formulae of the two chain isomers of C4H10 and name them.
questions.explanation: They are chain isomers because they differ in the arrangement of the carbon skeleton.

questions.q: What is a nucleophile? Give two examples.
questions.answer: A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates a pair of electrons to an electron-deficient centre, for example OH- and NH3 (also CN-).
questions.explanation: Nucleophile means nucleus-loving; it seeks a positively charged or partially positive atom.

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkene series?
questions.explanation: Alkenes with one double bond have the general formula CnH2n.

questions.q: Which reagent is used as a simple test for unsaturation in a hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: Unsaturated hydrocarbons decolourise the orange-brown bromine water by addition across the double or triple bond.

questions.q: What is the major product when HBr adds to propene in the absence of peroxide?
questions.explanation: By Markovnikov's rule hydrogen goes to the carbon with more hydrogens, so bromine attaches to the middle carbon.

questions.q: Benzene most characteristically undergoes
questions.explanation: The delocalised pi electron cloud attracts electrophiles, and substitution keeps the aromatic ring intact.

questions.q: Which of the following is aromatic according to Hückel's (4n + 2) pi electron rule?
questions.explanation: Benzene is planar, cyclic and fully conjugated with 6 pi electrons (n = 1); cyclobutadiene has 4 and cyclooctatetraene has 8.

questions.q: Write the equation of the Wurtz reaction for the preparation of ethane from bromomethane.
keyPoints: Alkyl halide treated with sodium metal
Two alkyl groups join to give a higher alkane
questions.explanation: Sodium removes the halogen and the two methyl groups couple to form a C-C bond.

questions.q: Explain why benzene is more stable than the hypothetical 'cyclohexatriene' with three fixed double bonds.
questions.answer: Benzene's pi electrons are delocalised over all six carbons (resonance), which lowers its energy; its resonance energy is about 150 kJ/mol and all C-C bonds are equal in length.
keyPoints: All C-C bonds equal, intermediate length
questions.explanation: The measured heat of hydrogenation of benzene is much lower than three times that of cyclohexene, showing extra stability.

questions.q: Why is a terminal alkyne such as ethyne more acidic than ethene or ethane?
questions.answer: The sp-hybridised carbon has 50% s-character and is more electronegative, so the C-H bond is more polarised and the acetylide ion is more stable.
keyPoints: More electronegative carbon holds the lone pair better
Terminal H can be removed by strong bases like NaNH2
questions.explanation: Greater s-character stabilises the negative charge on carbon in the conjugate base.
